output.query: hepatic encephalopathy West Haven grading precipitants lactulose rifaximin AASLD 2014

results.finding: HE is graded by the West Haven criteria (grades 0-IV). Grade II: lethargy, gross disorientation, asterixis. Grade III: somnolent but rousable, marked confusion. Diagnosis is clinical after excluding other causes of AMS. Serum ammonia is supportive but does not correlate well with grade; a normal or mildly elevated ammonia does not exclude HE. Lactulose (titrated to 2-4 stools per day) is first-line treatment. Rifaximin 550 mg twice daily as adjunct reduces recurrence. Precipitant identification and treatment are central to management.
results.title: Hepatic encephalopathy in chronic liver disease: 2014 Practice Guideline by AASLD and EASL

results.finding: Common precipitants of overt HE in cirrhosis include: constipation, dietary protein excess, GI hemorrhage, infection (especially SBP, UTI), hypokalemia, hyponatremia, dehydration, sedative medications (benzodiazepines, opioids), renal failure, and non-adherence with lactulose/rifaximin. Identification and reversal of the precipitant are as important as symptomatic treatment.
results.title: Hepatic encephalopathy

results.finding: Lactulose non-adherence is a frequent and underappreciated precipitant of overt HE in patients on secondary prophylaxis. Patients often discontinue lactulose when feeling well. Rifaximin reduces recurrence of overt HE. CNS depressants including benzodiazepines and opioids are contraindicated in HE as they worsen encephalopathy; haloperidol may be used for agitation at low doses.
results.title: Review article: the modern management of hepatic encephalopathy

alternatives: For pain management in this patient: acetaminophen at reduced hepatic dose (maximum 2 g/day) is preferred over opioids or NSAIDs
For nausea: ondansetron is preferred over promethazine in patients with liver disease
contraindications: Benzodiazepines are contraindicated in hepatic encephalopathy — markedly impaired hepatic clearance prolongs sedation and exacerbates encephalopathy
Opioid analgesics with hepatic metabolism (morphine, oxycodone, hydromorphone) are contraindicated in overt HE — unpredictable accumulation worsens consciousness level
Anticholinergic antiemetics (promethazine, metoclopramide in large doses) should be avoided in HE — additive CNS depression

prohibited_recommendations: Do not administer benzodiazepines or sedating opioids for agitation or anxiety — they precipitate and prolong HE in cirrhotic patients.
Do not attribute AMS to HE without first excluding infection (blood and urine cultures, SBP paracentesis) and structural intracranial pathology (CT head).
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect and hemorrhage in a patient with altered mental status.
Do not anchor on the mildly elevated ammonia (58 umol/L) as evidence against HE — ammonia correlates poorly with grade and a near-normal level does not exclude overt HE.
required_recommendations: Restart lactulose 30 mL every 4-6 hours initially, then titrate to 2-4 soft stools per day as first-line HE treatment.
Identify and address precipitants: treat constipation with lactulose and bowel regimen; confirm medication refill and adherence plan before discharge.
Diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP in any cirrhotic with ascites presenting with AMS, even without overt abdominal findings.
Monitor airway and mental status closely — escalate to ICU if GCS drops or airway protection is compromised.
Ensure no sedating CNS depressants are administered during hospitalization.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the acute HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute HE workup; the AMS is attributable to reversible metabolic encephalopathy, not Alzheimer pathology.
FDG-PET has no role in acute HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the clinical question, not paraneoplastic or neurodegenerative disease.
Formal neuropsychological testing cannot be validly performed during overt HE; indicated only for evaluation of minimal/covert HE after the acute episode resolves.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II-III), autoimmune hepatitis cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 13) — precipitated by constipation and lactulose non-adherence

differential.key_features: Ascites present — diagnostic paracentesis required to exclude SBP as concurrent precipitant; no fever or abdominal pain but SBP can be clinically silent
Thrombocytopenia (Plt 102) and elevated INR 1.5 increase bleeding risk; CT head excludes this
Electrolytes are normal in this case (Na 136, K 3.6); ruled out by labs
Creatinine and BUN both normal; renal failure excluded
Azathioprine does not cause encephalopathy at standard doses; on stable dose for years; excluded by clinical course and response to lactulose

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade II-III features (lethargy, disorientation, asterixis, GCS 12) in a known cirrhotic with a clear precipitant — constipation and 4-5 days of lactulose non-adherence — constitute sufficient basis for diagnosis after excluding alternate AMS causes.

The mildly elevated ammonia (58 umol/L, only slightly above the upper limit) is the key red herring: AASLD 2014 explicitly states ammonia does not correlate with HE grade and a near-normal level does not exclude overt HE. An agent anchoring on this value to dismiss or downgrade HE would err.

Normal electrolytes (Na 136, K 3.6, Mg 1.8), normal glucose, normal renal function, and negative cultures make electrolyte encephalopathy, hypoglycemia, and sepsis-driven AMS unlikely — the clinical picture narrows cleanly to HE from constipation and non-adherence.

Autoimmune hepatitis is an under-represented etiology in the HEP-ENC dataset; immunosuppressive maintenance (azathioprine + prednisone) is part of this patient's background but does not change the HE workup or immediate treatment.

Lactulose adherence counseling is integral to discharge planning — patients frequently stop lactulose when feeling well, making non-adherence the most common modifiable precipitant of recurrent overt HE.

SBP exclusion by paracentesis is mandatory in any cirrhotic patient with ascites and AMS, even without fever or abdominal pain, because SBP can present silently and is a life-threatening concurrent precipitant.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Serum ammonia correlates poorly with HE grade and a mildly elevated or near-normal value does not exclude overt HE (AASLD 2014). The diagnosis rests on clinical grounds: GCS 12, bilateral asterixis, disorientation, and a clear precipitant in a known cirrhotic. The ammonia supports but neither confirms nor excludes HE.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mrs. E. is a 67-year-old woman with autoimmune hepatitis cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) who was brought to the emergency department by her son after three days of worsening confusion and lethargy. Her son had called to check on her three days ago and noted she seemed unusually slow and repetitive on the phone. When he visited yesterday, he found her sleeping at midday, disoriented about the day of the week, and unable to recall a conversation from two hours earlier. She called her cat by a wrong name and left the front door unlocked overnight. This morning he could not rouse her to full alertness and brought her in.

On further history, the son reports that his mother had been complaining of constipation for approximately six days, attributing it to reduced dietary fiber and decreased fluid intake over the prior week because of poor appetite. She had not taken her lactulose doses for the past four to five days because she had run out and had not refilled the prescription — she had been feeling well recently and thought she could skip it temporarily. She had continued her rifaximin regularly. Her last bowel movement was four days ago. She denied dark stools, hematemesis, abdominal pain, or fever. No recent sick contacts, travel, or new medications. No falls or head trauma. There is no history of alcohol or recreational substance use.

Her prior HE episode eight months ago had resolved promptly with lactulose restart within 48 hours. Her hepatologist had emphasized strict lactulose adherence at that visit, but the patient had felt well and had a permissive attitude toward medication adherence. Review of systems is otherwise unremarkable except for mild nausea over the past week. She has no urinary symptoms.
